Real-world Software Disasters: High-Cost Software Failures
Ariane 5 Flight 501 (1996)
• Cost Impact: $370 Million lost in 37 seconds.
• Root Cause: Unhandled 64-bit to 16-bit integer overflow 
bug during flight path conversion.
• Core Issue: Reusing legacy flight code from Ariane 4 
without re-testing under Ariane 5's higher acceleration 
profile.
• Key Takeaway: Legacy code reuse requires rigorous 
regression and boundary testing under new operational 
contexts.
Boeing 737 MAX MCAS System (2018-
2019)
• Human & Financial Loss: 346 fatalities, over $20 Billion in 
direct corporate damages.
• Root Cause: MCAS flight control software relied on a 
single Angle of Attack (AoA) sensor without redundancy 
checks.
• Systemic Failure: Software lacked fault tolerance, Sensor 
validation, and pilot Override mechanisms.
• Key Takeaway: Critical safety software demands stringent 
SQA risk assessments and fail-safe design validation.

Why Software Has Bugs & The Defect Cost Curve (Rule of 10x)
Primary Causes of Software Defect
• Ambiguous & Changing Requirements: Missing edge-
case specifications early on.
• Human Miscommunication: Misalignment between 
Product Owners, Developers, and Testers.
• Code Complexity & Tight Deadlines: Rushed 
refactoring, technical debt, and architectural flaws.
• Environmental Factors: Hardware variability, third-party 
API dependencies, and legacy code integration.
Defect Cost Escalation (Rule of 10x)
• Requirements Phase: $1x cost to fix an error.
• Design & Coding Phase: $10x cost escalation.
• System Testing Phase: $100x cost to fix.
• Production / Post-Release: $1,000x to $10,000x cost + 
Severe Brand & Legal Damage.
• Core Takeaway: Shift-Left Testing (early defect detection) 
is essential for financial viability.

Definition & Core Focus of SQA
• Definition: Planned and systematic pattern of all actions 
necessary to provide adequate confidence that an item 
conforms to technical requirements.

• Primary Goal: DEFECT PREVENTION (Preventing

• Conducting Process Audits and Quality Reviews across

• Training team members on defect prevention techniques

Understanding Software Quality Control (SQC) & Testing
Software Quality Control (SQC)
• Definition: Set of activities designed to evaluate the 
quality of developed work products.
• Orientation: PRODUCT-ORIENTED.
• Goal: DEFECT DETECTION (Finding flaws in actual 
work deliverables).
• Activities: Code inspection, design reviews, technical 
walkthroughs, testing execution.

software under specified conditions to evaluate behavior 
and verify requirements.
• Focus: Dynamic execution of test suites against build 
releases.
• Core Objective: Identify defects, measure quality metrics, 
and build confidence prior to deployment.

Introduction to the 7 Principles of Software Testing (ISTQB v4.0)
Why Do Testing Principles Matter?
The International Software Testing Qualifications Board (ISTQB) defines 7 core principles that guide all testing activities.
Understanding these principles prevents unrealistic expectations (e.g., expecting 100% bug-free software) and optimizes test strategy.
1. Testing shows the presence of defects, not their absence.
2. Exhaustive testing is impossible.
3. Early testing saves time and money (Shift-Left).
4. Defects cluster together (80/20 Pareto Principle).
5. Beware of the pesticide paradox.
6. Testing is context dependent.
7. Absence-of-errors is a fallacy.

SOFTWARE QUALITY ASSURANCE & TESTING
Principles 1 & 2: Presence of Defects & Exhaustive Testing
Principle 1: Testing Shows Presence of 
Defects
• Core Concept: Testing can prove that defects exist in 
software, but cannot prove that software has ZERO 
defects.
• Misconception: 'The test suite passed 100%, so the 
system is totally bug-free.'
• Reality: Passing tests only mean no bugs were found 
under those specific tested conditions.
• Practical Action: Testing reduces probability of 
undiscovered defects remaining in production.
Principle 2: Exhaustive Testing is 
Impossible
• Core Concept: Testing ALL combinations of inputs, 
preconditions, and paths is mathematically impossible for 
non-trivial software.
• Example: A simple form with 10 text fields, each 
accepting 10 possible values, has 10^10 (10 Billion) 
combinations!
• Practical Action: Use Risk Analysis, Equivalence 
Partitioning, and Boundary Value Analysis to prioritize test 
execution.

SOFTWARE QUALITY ASSURANCE & TESTING
Principles 3 & 4: Early Testing & Defect Clustering
Principle 3: Early Testing (Shift-Left)
• Core Concept: Testing activities should start as early as 
possible in the SDLC (Static Testing on requirements).
• Why: Finding and fixing defects early costs a fraction of 
fixing them in production (Defect Cost Curve).
• Action: Conduct static reviews on User Stories, PRD 
documents, and System Architecture before coding 
starts.
Principle 4: Defect Clustering (80/20 
Rule)
• Core Concept: A small number of modules usually 
contain most of the defects discovered (Pareto Principle).
• Observation: ~80% of system defects are typically found 
in ~20% of core modules.
• Action: Identify high-risk, complex, or frequently modified 
modules and concentrate testing effort there.

SOFTWARE QUALITY ASSURANCE & TESTING
Principles 5 & 6: Pesticide Paradox & Context Dependency
Principle 5: Beware of Pesticide 
Paradox
• Core Concept: Re-running the exact same set of tests 
repeatedly will eventually fail to find new defects.
• Analogy: Overusing the same pesticide builds 
resistance in crop pests.
• Action: Periodically review, update, and write new test 
cases to exercise different paths and code regions.
Principle 6: Testing is Context Dependent
• Core Concept: Testing is performed differently in different 
contexts.
• Comparison:
- E-commerce App: Focus on performance, usability, and 
payment gateway load.
- Banking / FinTech: Focus on security, data encryption, 
and transactional compliance.
- Medical Device Software: Focus on safety compliance, 
reliability, and regulatory standards.

SOFTWARE QUALITY ASSURANCE & TESTING
Principle 7: Absence-of-Errors Fallacy (Verification vs. Validation)
Principle 7: Absence-of-Errors Fallacy
• Core Concept: Finding and fixing 100% of technical 
bugs does NOT guarantee a successful system.
• Why: If the system built does not fulfill user needs or 
business goals, it will fail in the marketplace.
• Example: A software application that works flawlessly 
without crashing, but has an unusable UI that confuses 
customers.
Verification vs. Validation
• Verification (Xác minh): 'Are we building the product 
RIGHT?'
- Focus: Checking conformance with written 
specifications and technical design.
• Validation (Xác nhận): 'Are we building the RIGHT 
product?'
- Focus: Checking whether the product meets actual user 
needs and business expectations.

Software Testing Life Cycle (STLC) & Entry/Exit Criteria
What is STLC?
• Definition: Sequence of specific testing activities 
executed to ensure software quality goals are met.
• Structure: Comprises 6 distinct sequential & overlapping 
phases.
• Systematic Approach: Each phase has defined 
objectives, deliverables, and quality gates.
Entry Criteria vs. Exit Criteria Rule
• Entry Criteria: Essential prerequisites and items that 
MUST be completed before a phase can start.
- Example: SRS document approved before Test Planning 
starts.
• Exit Criteria: mandatory conditions and results that MUST 
be fulfilled before a phase is declared complete.
- Example: 100% Critical bugs closed before Test 
Closure.

STLC Phase 2: Test Planning & IEEE 829 Standard
Test Planning Activities

• Activities:

Phase 5: Test Execution

• Activities:

Case Study: Intel Pentium FDIV Bug (1994)
The Floating-Point Division Failure
• The Bug:
The Intel Pentium chip returned extremely small errors 
in complex float calculations.
• Technical Root Cause:
A lookup table in the SRT division hardware algorithm 
was missing exactly 5 constants (entered as 0 instead 
of +2) due to an off-by-one compiler loop condition.
• Intel's System Testing Approach:
Intel ran millions of randomized floating-point 
operations at the system level. The error probability 
was 1 in 9 billion, so system tests completely missed 
it.
The Essential Testing Takeaway
• The Illusion of 'Full System Testing':
Intel assumed massive system-level runs made lower 
testing redundant. But system testing is black-box and 
cannot probe isolated, deep micro-logic paths.
• The Unit Testing Solution (Ammann & Offutt):
If Intel had run basic Unit Testing with simple code 
coverage criteria (such as branch or statement 
coverage) on the SRT module, the 5 missing states 
would have been exposed instantly.
• Hậu quả (Financial & Brand Disaster):
Intel was forced to issue a comprehensive recall, 
costing over $475 million and severely damaging its 
reputation.

Case Study: NASA Mars Climate Orbiter (1999)
The $327M Communication Breakdown
• The Incident:
In September 1999, the Mars Climate Orbiter entered 
orbit too low and burned up in the Martian 
atmosphere.
• The Interface Mismatch:
A ground-based thruster software module (Lockheed 
Martin) outputted thrust values in English units 
(Pound-force-seconds). The spacecraft flight control 
module (NASA JPL) expected metric units (Newton-
seconds).
• Status of Individual Modules:
Both software modules passed their own Unit Testing 
with 100% correct logic. They only failed when 
transmitting data to each other.
The Need for Integration Testing
• A Classic Integration Fault:
This is the ultimate textbook example of an 
Integration/Interface defect. It was caused by conflicting 
assumptions on parameter boundaries and types.
• Interface Data Flow Testing:
Integration testing must track the coupling of 
parameters. Ensuring that variables defined in the caller 
unit are correctly consumed by the callee unit would 
have caught this unit-mismatch immediately.
• Core Lesson:
Even if every single developer claims 'my code works 
100% independently', the system can still crash upon 
assembly.

Test Level 1: Unit Testing - Foundation
Understanding Unit Testing
• Definition of a 'Unit':
The smallest testable, contiguous block of source code (e.g., 
helper functions in C/Python, class methods in Java/C#).
• Primary Objectives:
Isolate and verify the internal logic of a single function, ensuring 
it handles boundary values, empty states, and traps exceptions.
• Primary Owner:
Software Developers (Developers) are responsible for 
designing, executing, and maintaining unit tests.
Technical Implementation & Tools
• White-box Focus:
Derived strictly from source code structure. 
Focuses on code coverage metrics:
- Statement Coverage (every line run)
- Branch Coverage (every true/false choice 
executed)
- Path/Condition Coverage (individual sub-
clauses evaluated)
• Standard Automation Frameworks:
JUnit (Java), pytest (Python), Mocha/Jest 
(JavaScript), xUnit (.NET). Unit tests are kept with 
the code and run on every save/commit.

Unit Testing in Object-Oriented Systems
In Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), encapsulation blurs the boundaries between methods and classes. Unit testing shifts from 
testing isolated functions to verifying classes and object state behaviors.
The 4 OO Testing Tiers
1. Intra-method Testing:
Testing a single isolated method within a class (basic 
unit test).
2. Inter-method Testing:
Testing interactions of method pairs in the same class.
3. Intra-class Testing:
Testing a single class as a whole through chains of 
method calls that mutate the object's internal state 
(State-based testing).
4. Inter-class Testing:
Testing relationships between multiple classes (enters 
Integration Test).

Test Level 2: Integration Testing - Interfaces
Understanding Integration Testing
• Primary Objective:
Detect defects arising from the interface interactions and data 
communication flow between correctly functioning modules.
• Focus Area: The Interfaces:
Assumes individual components are structurally sound and 
isolates compatibility, data flow, and messaging sequence 
errors.
• Core Basis:
Subsystem Architecture Designs, Database schemas, API 
contracts (OpenAPI/Swagger documents).
Common Integration-Level Faults
• Data Type Mismatch:
Caller passes Float but Callee expects Double. 
Mismatch in units (e.g. Pound vs. Newton).
• Sequencing Constraints:
API called in wrong order (e.g., trying to write() 
data to a file before running open() first).
• Shared Resource Conflict:
Race conditions and memory leaks on global DB 
connections or cache layers.
• Serialization Errors:
Wrong JSON field names or malformed XML 
structures during HTTP calls.

Integration Strategies: Assembling Systems
1. Big Bang Integration
• Process: Connect all completed modules simultaneously and 
test as one block.
• Risk: Very dangerous. If a failure occurs, locating the root 
cause is a debugging nightmare. Suitable only for trivial projects.
2. Top-Down Integration
• Process: Test high-level UI/control modules first, going down 
the hierarchy.
• Scaffolding: Requires STUBS (dummy helper functions) to 
mock unbuilt lower-level calculation units. Exposes core system 
architecture early.
3. Bottom-Up Integration
• Process: Test low-level utilities and DB structures first, moving 
up to the UI.
• Scaffolding: Requires DRIVERS (temporary test scripts) to call 
and feed data to lower modules. Ensures foundation is robust 
first.
4. Sandwich / API-First Integration
• Sandwich: Combines top-down and bottom-up testing around a 
central middle layer.
• API-First: Modern industry standard. Focuses on 
REST/GraphQL HTTP integration between microservices via 
Postman or automated integration tests.

Execution Strategy: Re-Testing vs. Regression
Re-Testing (Confirmation)
• Single Goal:
Validates if a previously reported bug has been 
successfully resolved by the development team.
• Scope: Very Narrow:
Executes exactly the same test step/script that failed 
previously. Focuses only on the bug area.
• Timing:
Run immediately after receiving a new software build 
containing the specific hotfix.
Regression Testing (Safety Net)
• Single Goal:
Guarantees that new code additions or hotfixes did not 
break existing features.
• Scope: Broad & Global:
Covers all surrounding modules, related data paths, 
and core system functionality.
• Golden QA Rule:
After any RE-TEST is completed successfully, a 
REGRESSION TEST must be run to prevent side-
effects in other system areas.
Software Quality Assurance & Testing Principles (SE302-M)  |  Session 2  |  Slide 19/28

Regression Testing in Practice & Automation
Managing Growing Test Suites
• The Regression Bottleneck:
As software grows, the regression test suite expands 
exponentially. Manual execution becomes impossible within 
short release cycles.
• Selective Regression Strategies:
Instead of 'Retest-All', teams select tests based on:
- Code Impact Analysis: Trace changed lines to 
corresponding tests.
- Risk-based prioritization: Always test high-risk billing and 
login systems first.
Automation & Integration
• The Savior: Automation Testing:
Regression testing is the primary target for 
automated scripts. It runs repetitive, predictable 
tests continuously.
• Continuous Integration (CI/CD):
Automated suites (Selenium, Playwright, Cypress) 
are triggered on every code merge to catch 
regressions instantly before deployment.
• Business Value:
Prevents regression bugs from escaping to 
production, lowering the cost of hotfixes.

Execution Strategy: Smoke vs. Sanity Testing
Smoke Testing (Build Verification)
• Objective: Verify Build Stability:
Ensures the new build is stable enough for the testing 
team to accept and run deep tests.
• Scope: Broad but Shallow:
Evaluates only core critical features (e.g., login, 
loading homepage, basic checkout).
• Build Rejection Rule:
If Smoke Test fails (e.g. system crashes on login), 
reject the build immediately. This saves QA resources 
from testing a broken system.
Sanity Testing (Quick Sanity Check)
• Objective: Minor Fix Verification:
Performs a quick sanity check to verify if a specific 
hotfix behaves reasonably.
• Scope: Narrow but Deep:
Deeply tests only the specific modified block and its 
immediate dependencies.
• Fast Feedback:
Quickly validates minor code modifications before 
releasing or conducting full regression suites.

WHAT IS DEFECT LIFE CYCLE?
• New:When a defect is logged and posted for the first time. Its state is given as new.
• Assigned: Once the bug is posted by the tester, the lead of the tester approves the bug and 
assigns the bug to developer team.
• Open: Its state when the developer starts analyzing and working on the defect fix.
• Fixed: When developer makes necessary code changes and verifies the changes then he/she can 
make bug status as ‘Fixed’.
• Retest: At this stage the tester do the retesting of the changed code which developer has given to 
him to check whether the defect got fixed or not.
• Reopened: If the bug still exists even after the bug is fixed by the developer, the tester changes 
the status to “reopened”. The bug goes through the life cycle once again.

WHAT IS DEFECT LIFE CYCLE?
• Deferred:The bug, changed to deferred state means the bug is expected to be fixed in next releases. 
The reasons for changing the bug to this state have many factors. Some of them are a priority the bug 
may be low, lack of time for the release or the bug may not have a major effect on the software.
• Rejected: If the developer feels that the bug is not genuine, the developer rejects the bug. Then the 
state of the bug is changed to “rejected”.
• Duplicate : If the bug is repeated twice or the two bugs mention the same concept of the bug, then 
the recent/latest bug status is changed to “duplicate“.
• Closed: Once the bug is fixed, it is tested by the tester. If the tester feels that the bug no longer exists in 
the software, tester changes the status of the bug to “closed”. This state means that the bug is fixed, 
tested and approved.

WHAT IS DEFECT LIFE CYCLE?
• Not a bug/Enhancement: The state given as “Not a bug/Enhancement” if there is no change in 
the functionality of the application. For an example: If customer asks for some change in the look 
and field of the application like change of color of some text then it is not a bug but just some 
change in the looks of the application.
Conclusion:
• A Bug is the result of a coding Error and A Defect is a deviation from the Requirements. A 
defect does not necessarily mean there is a bug in the code, it could be a function that was 
not implemented but defined in the requirements of the software.

• Bug/Defect severity can be defined as the impact of the bug on the application. It can be

• Severity can be categorized into three types:
• As mentioned above the type of severity are categorized as Critical, Major, and Minor
• Let’s see how can we segregate a bug into these types:

BUG SEVERITY AND PRIORITY 
• Critical:
• A critical severity issue is an issue where a large piece of functionality or major system component is completely broken and there 
is no workaround to move further.
For example, Due to a bug in one module, we cannot test the other modules because that blocker bug has blocked the other 
modules. Bugs which affects the customers business are considered as critical
• Major:
• A major severity issue is an issue where a large piece of functionality or major system component is completely broken and there
is a workaround to move further.
• Minor:
• A minor severity issue is an issue that imposes some loss of functionality, but for which there is an acceptable & easily reproducible 
workaround.
• For example, font family or font size or color or spelling issue
• Trivial:
• A trivial severity defect is a defect which is related to the enhancement of the system

BUG SEVERITY AND PRIORITY 
• What is Priority?
• Defect priority can be defined as an impact of the bug on the customers business. Main focus on how soon the defect should be fixed. It 
gives the order in which a defect should be resolved. Developers decide which defect they should take up next based on the priority. It can 
be High, Medium or Low.
• Most of the times the priority status is set based on the customer requirement.
• High:
• A high priority issue is an issue which has a high impact on the customers business or an issue which affects the system seve rely and the 
system cannot be used until the issue was fixed. These kinds of issues must be fixed immediately. Most of the cases as per the user 
perspective, the priority of the issue is set to high priority even though the severity of the issue is minor.
• Medium:
• Issues which can be released in the next build comes under medium priority. Such issues can be resolved along with other development 
activities.
• Low:
• An issue which has no impact on the customer business comes under low priority.

WHAT IS DEFECT LIFE CYCLE?
• New:When a defect is logged and posted for the first time. Its state is given as new.
• Assigned: Once the bug is posted by the tester, the lead of the tester approves the bug and 
assigns the bug to developer team.
• Open: Its state when the developer starts analyzing and working on the defect fix.
• Fixed: When developer makes necessary code changes and verifies the changes then he/she can 
make bug status as ‘Fixed’.
• Retest: At this stage the tester do the retesting of the changed code which developer has given to 
him to check whether the defect got fixed or not.
• Reopened: If the bug still exists even after the bug is fixed by the developer, the tester changes 
the status to “reopened”. The bug goes through the life cycle once again.

WHAT IS DEFECT LIFE CYCLE?
• Deferred:The bug, changed to deferred state means the bug is expected to be fixed in next releases. 
The reasons for changing the bug to this state have many factors. Some of them are a priority the bug 
may be low, lack of time for the release or the bug may not have a major effect on the software.
• Rejected: If the developer feels that the bug is not genuine, the developer rejects the bug. Then the 
state of the bug is changed to “rejected”.
• Duplicate : If the bug is repeated twice or the two bugs mention the same concept of the bug, then 
the recent/latest bug status is changed to “duplicate“.
• Closed: Once the bug is fixed, it is tested by the tester. If the tester feels that the bug no longer exists in 
the software, tester changes the status of the bug to “closed”. This state means that the bug is fixed, 
tested and approved.

WHAT IS DEFECT LIFE CYCLE?
• Not a bug/Enhancement:The state given as “Not a bug/Enhancement” if there is no change in 
the functionality of the application. For an example: If customer asks for some change in the look 
and field of the application like change of color of some text then it is not a bug but just some 
change in the looks of the application.

I. Structural Database T esting
Structural Database T estingis a database testing technique that validates all the elements inside 
data repository that are mainly used for data storage and which are not allowed to be directly 
manipulated by end-users. The validation of database servers is also an important consideration in 
structural database testing. A successful completion of this testing needs mastery in SQL queries.
a) Schema T estingin database testing validates various schema formats associated with the 
database and verifies whether the mapping formats of tables/views/columns are compatible 
with mapping formats of user interface. The main purpose of schema testing is to ensure the 
schema mapping between front-end and back-end are similar. Thus, it is also referred to 
as mapping testing.
▪ Validation of the various schema formats associated with the databases. Many times the 
mapping format of the table may not be compatible with the mapping format present in 
the user interface level of the application.

DATABASE TESTING
a) Database Load testing
The purpose of any load test should be clearly understood and documented. The following types of 
configurations are a must for load testing.
• The most frequently used user transactions have the potential to impact the performance of all of the 
other transactions if they are not efficient.
• At least one non-editing user transaction should be included in the final test suite, so that performance of 
such transactions can be differentiated from other more complex transactions.
• The more important transactions that facilitate the core objectives of the system should be included, as 
failure under a load of these transactions has, by definition, the greatest impact.
• At least one editable transaction should be included so that performance of such transactions can be 
differentiated from other transactions.
• Optimum response time under huge number of virtual users for all the prospective requirements.
• Effective times for fetching of various records.
